title: Which party will win the most seats in the 2026 Israeli election?
resolution_criteria: This question will resolve as the political party that receives more seats than any other in the 2026 Israeli legislative election, scheduled to take place on October 27, 2026.
fine_print:
If a party other than Likud or Yashar wins a plurality of seats, the question will resolve as **Other.** If the elections are canceled or postponed such that results are unavailable before January 1, 2027, the question will be **annulled**.

In the event of a tie, the question resolves as the party of the next prime minister of the first government formed after the election, or (if the PM is from another party) as the tied party with at least one other minister in the government, pursuant to section 13(d) or section 13A(e) of Basic Law: The Government ([pdf](https://main.knesset.gov.il/EN/activity/documents/BasicLawsPDF/BasicLawTheGovernment.pdf)).  In case more than one tied party is represented, the PM is from some other party, no party is represented, or  in case no government is formed, then the question resolves as the tied party that receives the most officially reported votes in the election.
background:
Elections are scheduled for October 27, 2026, to determine the makeup of the 26th Knesset, the legislature of Israel. [Polling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opinion_polling_for_the_2026_Israeli_legislative_election) in recent months suggests a close race between the two leading parties, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's [Likud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Likud) and [Yashar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yashar_\(political_party\)), a new centrist party that was formed in 2025 by [Gadi Eisenkot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gadi_Eisenkot), a former government minister and Israel Defense Forces (IDF) chief of staff.

As a newly created party, Yashar currently holds no seats in the Knesset. Likud, by contrast, is a longstanding major player in Israeli politics, having been formed in 1973 and in government for most of Israel's recent history. Likud currently holds 32 seats, more than any other party, and leads the current government.

comments.author: sai_39
comments.text:
I disagree with the crowd albeit slightly. Likud could have a slightly higher probability. The latest major polls look roughly like this:

| Poll / date                        | Yashar | Likud | Gap       |
| ---------------------------------- | ------ | ----- | --------- |
| Zman Yisrael/Tatika, Sept 30–Oct 1 | 21     | 21    | 0         |
| Channel 13, \~Sept 30              | 21     | 19    | Yashar +2 |
| Kan, Sept 28                       | 23     | 21    | Yashar +2 |
| N12, late Sept                     | 23     | 20    | Yashar +3 |
| Maariv, late Sept                  | 22     | 18    | Yashar +4 |
| i24NEWS, late Sept                 | 22     | 27    | Likue +5  |

The [Oct. 1 Zman poll](https://www.timesofisrael.com/liveblog_entry/toi-poll-netanyahus-bloc-leads-likud-tied-for-1st-as-voters-fret-over-elections-outcome/) had 500 respondents and a ±4.4 percentage-point sampling margin; it put Likud and Yashar exactly level at 21 seats. [Channel 13's poll](https://www.timesofisrael.com/liveblog_entry/netanyahu-led-bloc-regains-lead-in-tv-poll-but-remains-well-short-of-knesset-majority/) around the same time had Yashar 21–19 over Likud, with a much larger sample of 1,013 and a reported ±2.5-point margin. The [divergence between pollsters](https://www.jpost.com/israel-election-2026/article-909804) is striking. In one recent five-poll comparison, Likud ranged from 18 to 32 seats, while Yashar was much more stable at 22–23. That comparison's simple average was Likud 23, Yashar 22.2, but a lot of that Likud average came from the much more Likud-friendly [Channel 14](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Channel_14_\(Israel\)#Inside_Israel) and i24 polls.

[Reuters' polling tracker](https://www.reuters.com/graphics/ISRAEL-ELECTION/POLLS/lgvdbwrakvo/), using polls through Sept. 28 and smoothing individual polls with local polynomial regression, likewise described the top-two gap as only about **one seat**.

There are several moving pieces:

1\) Eisenkot's initial surge has stopped expanding. For example, the Sept. 28 Kan poll moved Yashar from 24 to 23 while Likud went from 20 to 21; Bennett's B'Yachad continued declining to 11. [Jerusalem Post](https://www.jpost.com/israel-election-2026/article-909918) 
The Oct. 1 Zman poll then had Eisenkot at only 21, down from earlier figures in the mid-20s.

2\) Second, Netanyahu has managed to return the campaign to terrain he has historically emphasized: security, external threats and his ability to deal with hostile actors. [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/using-old-election-playbook-netanyahu-projects-image-israels-protector-despite-2026-09-29/) described his current campaign as deliberately reviving his longstanding "protector of Israel" pitch, despite the obvious vulnerability created by October 7 happening on his watch. 

3\) There's a potentially damaging counter-story. Reports have alleged that Netanyahu received warnings from Egyptian and Emirati officials before October 7 and did not appropriately transmit them. Netanyahu emphatically denies receiving such warnings. The dispute has become a major campaign issue, although analysts quoted by the [FT questioned](https://www.ft.com/content/f261c9cd-7169-4d16-97fc-9859099ce0f8) how many votes it can move because views of Netanyahu are already highly polarized.

4\) The Arab-party issue remains extremely important for government formation but less directly important for "largest party." Israel's Supreme Court [overturned attempts](https://www.ft.com/content/9bbcd715-1417-49b6-bc56-1745f17cd674) to disqualify the two principal Arab lists, while Sami Abu Shehadeh subsequently [withdrew](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/israeli-court-pressure-pushes-israeli-arab-leader-quit-election-race-2026-10-02/) after the court indicated it was inclined to uphold his personal disqualification.

**A few dark-horse, controversial observations:**

1. The flydubai cockpit attack is unusually well-timed politically, given the parallel allegations that Netanyahu ignored pre-Oct. 7 warnings. Though there is no evidence connecting the two.
2. US incentives are worth watching, but Eisenkot is hardly a dove: he remains hawkish on Iran, wants Hamas removed, and opposes Palestinian statehood, while appearing more open than Netanyahu to US-backed diplomacy and alternative governance in Gaza.

comments.author: sai_39
comments.text: @(Theomachado) Channel 14 is pretty clearly [right-wing/pro-Netanyahu](https://www.timesofisrael.com/liveblog_entry/netanyahu-shared-campaign-ad-claiming-rivals-will-persecute-right-wingers-close-media-outlets/), while [i24](https://mediabiasfactcheck.com/i24-news/) is also often characterized as right-leaning, though that label is somewhat more contested. More importantly, the two polling series [aren't entirely independent](https://israelpolicyforum.org/2026/08/20/israeli-election-polls-pollsters/): i24 uses Direct Polls, while Channel 14's polling is run by Shlomo Filber, who previously ran Direct Polls. I agree that treating the 27–31 Likud numbers as a separate polling camp makes sense!

comments.author: DeRuina
comments.text: I think the resolution's tie-break rule deserves more attention than it's getting. The last two mainstream polls (Kan, 27 September; Channel 12, 23 September) have Yashar ahead of Likud by only two to three seats, comfortably inside normal Israeli polling error, and Likud has a history of matching or beating its final polls (2015 and 2020 are the obvious cases). The spread across pollsters is also unusually wide: Direct Polls (9 September) had Likud 27–22 and Channel 14 has had Likud up by ten, so the "Yashar leads" reading depends on which house you trust. A Yashar-Likud seat tie is therefore a live scenario, not a rounding error. Under this question, a tie doesn't go to "Other" and isn't split; it resolves to whichever party leads or joins the first government, and only then to raw votes. With the blocs at 52-52, Netanyahu is at least as well placed as Eisenkot to assemble that first government. If you agree, a small slice of probability should move from Yashar to Likud purely on tie mechanics. In a 52-52 tie, which party's leader do you think has the better path to the first coalition?

comments.author: DaiLothbrook
comments.text: First, this is not a question I intend to spend much attention on. I find it difficult even to discuss Israel given what I regard as its ongoing war crimes and democratic erosion. Nevertheless, I will try to separate that moral judgment from my forecasting assessment. I have low confidence in the reliability of polling and political information produced under the present conditions, so the eventual result could differ substantially from both this forecast and the community consensus. Having said that, I currently give Yashar 55%, Likud 40% and another party 5%. Most recent polls favor Yashar, but the disagreement among pollsters leaves considerable room for error.
